sections.content:
The course is a standard introductory finance course.
It covers topics such as time value of money, interest rates, bonds, stocks, financial statement analysis, capital budgeting, risk and return, and cost of capital. The content is not too difficult if you have some basic math background, but the summer term schedule can feel a bit rushed near the end.
sections.teaching:
Professor SAENYASIRI is generally a decent professor.
He usually starts the lecture by discussing recent financial news, which makes the class more interesting, although it is not very related to the exams. His accent may take some time to get used to, but the main ideas are still understandable. The lectures are quite interactive, and he often asks students questions.
sections.grading: The grading is based on participation, assignments, midterm, and final exam. Participation marks are not hard to get if you answer his questions or Mentimeter questions. The assignments are done through Pearson MyLab Finance and are quite manageable, but you need to buy the textbook/access code. Both exams are multiple choice, and one A4 cheat sheet is allowed, so preparing a good cheat sheet with formulas and sample questions is very useful.
sections.workload: The workload is light overall. Assignments are not difficult and can usually be finished quickly. However, the 4-hour lectures in summer term can be tiring, and the course moves quite fast. Overall, it is a manageable course as long as you keep up with the materials and prepare well before exams.

sections.teaching:
Professor Saenyasiri has a very strong Thai accent. His voice is very sharp as well. Frankly, his voice irritates my ears after a while. You can still understand what he is saying, but the accent is definitely severe.  His teaching style itself is pretty normal. It is not incredibly entertaining, but it isn’t super boring either. He is interactive and constantly asking students questions. Since it is a four-hour long class, he will give around two to three breaks to us.

For the lectures, he actually starts every class by going over the latest global finance news. While it is a nice way to stay informed about what is happening in the world, but it is completely unrelated to the actual course content or exams. Sometimes, he skips over certain slides and telling the class that we can handle it on our own. Fortunately, the material isn't too overwhelming, and it really is manageable to just look over those by yourself.

As for his exams, I think it's fair. On our midterm, the class average was lower than he expected, so he actually adjusted the scores and added a few points to everyone's grade.

sections.content:
First of all, I have never studied in any other business courses before. I have zero background about it (pure science background). However, I think this course is not too difficult for those who has no business background before (as long as you work on it!).

It is quite normal that you feel confused about the terms and concepts as you begin to learn it but trust me, you can get through it before midterm!

The structure of this course is based on 'week', for each week, a new chapter was learnt (except week 4 and 5, which focused on ch4 only). So there were 11 chapters covered. These 11 chapters come from textbook 'Corporate Finance: Core Principles and Applications (6th edition)', it is a must to buy it cuz you gonna do homework in it's connect system.

This course basically teaches you how to read balance sheet and income statement, how to extract info from these statements, the concept of Cash Flow, stocks and bonds, to see how a much a company worth, how money depreciate as time gone by (most important concept through the course!), how to buy stocks etc. You'll encounter a lot of calculation stuff + conceptual stuff. Good news: chapters are coherent so you can consolidate your learning as you work through it.

Here's the outline:
Week 1: chapter 1: Introduction to Corporate Finance

Week 2: Chapter 3: Financial Statement Analysis & Financial Models

Week 3: Chapter 2: Financial Statements & Cash Flow

Week 4: Chapter 4: Discounted Cash Flow Valuation

Week 5: Chapter 4: Discounted Cash Flow Valuation

Week 6: Chapter 5: Interest Rates and Bond Valuation

Week 7: Midterm (21/3)

Week 11: Midterm break

Week 13: Chapter 12: Risk, Cost of Capital, and Capital Budgeting

Final Exam (23/5)

By the way, besides ordinary lecture stuff, they also provided a 'game': Portfolio Management Game. It is just a stock market simulation, if you buy good stocks, you'll earn game coins. Besides, doing good in weekly quizzes and in-class polling iPRS can also increase game coins.

Game coins can in turn help you with you your mini quizzes result if you earn a lot of it. (Yes! So if you do well in mini quizzes, you earn more game coins, more game coins help you do better in mini quizzes, positive cycle!)

sections.teaching:
This semester we are having different approach. There will be a routine work for each week: Textbook readings -> VOS (voice-over slides) -> ICA (in-class activity) -> Lesson -> mini-quiz. We have one lesson only every week.

Textbook reading: I don't know it is my problem or not, the textbook is quite difficult to understand and missing reasoning behind formulas. It is important to read the textbook because his notes will not cover all the materials in the book. (They will be examined!)

VOS and lecture notes: Basically VOS  goes through the set of lecture notes for that week. VOS is fine but the lecture notes design is horrible. I do think these notes are made in 1990s. There is no layout, a bunch of irrelevant graphics and "colourful" content. How colourful is that? In week2 material, there couple of slides taking about all the formulas for the ratios. First it is overwhelming. Second, everything is squeeze in one page like it costs him 1million to insert a new slide. (Those formulas are NOT important!)
ALSO HE LOVES SHORT FORM SO MUCH. Let's play a game if you have studied ACCT2010:
Q1: what RV stands for? (Revenue, easy)
Q2: what TX stands for? (Tax)
Q3: what is INT??? (not integer! but interest expense! maybe you will mess up this one with inventory?)
Confusing right?
The first few weeks are all like this :)
Even I got an A in Acct2010, I still suffer from all these mess,

Regular lesson: Something quite nice about this prof is that he plans to have a Portfolio Management Game (PMG) that allows everyone to invest in different stocks in the real world and earn GameCoins. Options like shorting are allowed which is quite fascinating. Every lesson, he will spend some time reviewing the trend of this week. During Chinese New Year he even gives out LaiSee/chocolate coin to the best players or the one actively answering questions. Quite Nice.
There will be an In Class Activity every week and most of them are either case analysis to this week's topic or illustrate some important points in VOS/lecture notes. Overall it is quite good to have his lessons. There will be some IPRS questions for students to win GameCoin for PMG. So no attendance is required.

Mini-quiz: usually mini-quiz consists of basic question or some IPRS question of that week. You will start feeling that some questions are hard to answer, and that is the most difficult part of this course, students admitted to this course are coming from other school like taking business minor or majoring in MAEC/MATH SF track. The math in this course is super easy for us. Therefore, Prof loves those "concept" questions rather than computation. (TA said this)

TA Kenrick is helpful. For those local students who have no accounting background. Attend the optional tutorial and ask Kenrick in Cantonese. The first few chapters will definitely destroy your passion in this course.

sections.content:
The content of this course is divided into 3 main parts:
1. time value of money (PV,FV,PMT,I)
2. capital budgeting
3. risk and return

As long as you have build up a good foundation in these concepts, you will have no problem understanding the worked examples as well as the narrower concepts established from the main parts. Having a good understanding of the lecture notes provided should be enough to get you a B or above. It's rather difficult to get A range unless you put in a lot of effort in reading the textbook and understanding every solution to the homework.
sections.teaching:
The professor delivers the course materials fairly concisely. As the slides combine both concept and worked solutions, the professor usually just goes through the slides relatively quickly.

However, sometimes she tends to spend quite a lot of time explaining the solution (for the 1% bonus mark question) even when similar question types have already been explained.
sections.grading:

15% homework
30% midterm
45% final

The mean for the midterm was around 70%, while for the final the mean was about 78%. Make sure you get the 15% in the homework and 10% of attendance as they are the easiest.
sections.workload: Not much workload. Around 10 homework in total, 1 given per week. No need to go to tutorial as the slides will be uploaded to canvas (with detailed solutions).

sections.content: Content is relevant and good. Heavily relies on the Pearson book. Covers basics of capital budgeting, basic models for pricing financial instruments and investment decision rules. The course wraps really well on itself towards the end and everything makes sense and fits together well.
sections.teaching: Really liked the instructor. Very easy to approach, hands out notes throughout the course and appeared to be extremely knowledgeable. Though I disliked his approach of not covering every single topic, but instead telling students to read it from the book. I think that was terrible, but thankfully these topics were not quantitative nor difficult, so this was not a problem in the end.
sections.grading: More than fair. There were 2 quizzes, a midterm and a final, plus some MyFinanceLab (online) homework. The online homework was not really graded, one just had to try to do exercises for full marks. Quizzes and exams overall were 99% multiple choice questions and overall not very difficult. A Financial calculator could be useful and would make a lot of things faster, though I didn't get one myself. Got an A- overall. The curve is pretty harsh at least with our class as the level was quite high. Attendance is needed.
sections.workload: Not too bad. The online MyFinanceLab homework is released weekly but is quite easy to do. Studying for finals, MT and quizzes I would consider is necessary, but certainly nothing impossible.

Also explains quite slow, which results in him asking us to study some chapters all by ourselves (but it's all theories).
Asks a lot of calculation questions for his exams and theories are mostly based on understanding with a bit of memorization.

But the tutorial is amazing, recommend going to his every tutorial if you have time.

The assignments account for 45% and final account for another 50%. Assignments are above mean but final should be below mean and turn out it is a C- grade.

sections.content: This course is designed for non-SBM students to learn about the basic concepts in Coporate Finance. It includes the most basic things like Time Value of Money, Balance Sheet, Income Statement. Later it talks about the knowledge of finance market like bonds, stocks. In general, the content is plentiful and useful in life, to help you better aware of what's happening in the real finance market around the world.
sections.teaching: Mainland students like to call the professor "一卡柴", since the pronunciation is pretty the same as his family name. He is very friendly and helpful, willing to answer any questions about the content. As the head of QFin department, his profession is well-accepted. He could explain a concept clearly, sometimes supplemented by hand-drawing. But he may stick to a student's question or an easy concept for too long in the class time and fail to complete the chapter as scheduled, and later have to accelerate in teaching, making us confused of some knowledge.
sections.grading:
Similar as many SBM courses. There's a 3% participation in the grading, every correct PRS answer gives 0.1%, and raising hands to ask questions brings you 0.5%. If you attend all the classes, the PRS part should be enough. There are two midterms and one final. The homework part is online, and super easy to get high marks if you cooperate with others to avoid silly mistakes. The grading is as follows: midterm1: 22%
+midterm2: 30%+final30%+HW15%+participation3%
i can't quite remember how the professor finally assign the grade,(maybe curving) but it's not so good from my friends' opinion.
Generally I think the grading is fair and the grade is  not so hard.
sections.workload: I would suggest to read the chapters in the textbooks thoroughly, before the scheduled class. And there will also be questions in exam to include book knowledge, which are not mentioned in the class. Reading the book takes most of my time on this course. The workload is not so big if you treat it as kind of a 'major' course, but not merely a CCC.
